transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Democrats gathered in Denver for a conference that was half victory party, half look ahead at how to deliver for voters.
As NPR's Barbara Sprant reports, the event brought together rising stars, organizers, and lawmakers.
Speaker after speaker said Democrats can't rest on their laurels.
Here's former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg.
It is yet to be written whether what we just experienced is one more oscillation from one side to the other and back,
or whether it is the beginning of a tectonic movement changing American politics.
He said Democrats should come out of the gate strong with a rapid-fire series of bills to lower the cost of living.
He was one of many potential presidential candidates in attendance,
all of whom said they're taking their time to decide before officially throwing their hat in the ring.
Barbara Sprant, NPR News, Denver.
More than 10,000 flights were delayed or canceled today, according to Flight Tracker FlightAware,
as thousands of passengers are still stranded after yesterday's hours-long ground stop.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says a federal contractor who is changing out copper wire for fiber optics may be to blame.
Former DOT Inspector General Mary Schiavo says the contractor was doing software patches work,
which caused the system to reboot, causing the crash.
She says it was running on a router made some 20 years ago.
This has happened before, and most coincidentally, or rather as in reading a crystal ball,
the Government Accountability Office on September 14, 2026 predicted exactly this.
They said without some major change, the FAA will once again repeat its history of cost-over runs and missed deadlines.
Schiavo speaking there to NPR's Weekend Edition.
Workers in New York City are still removing rubble from the Brooklyn Building collapse that killed at least eight people Wednesday,
and Piers de Waalice Saikavto has more.
Trucks have been hauling away large containers filled with rubble from the collapsed three-story apartment building,
a small makeshift memorial of candles and flowers sits on the corner of Bedford and Flatbush Avenue here.
Kishonna Landis lives nearby. She says she feels developers should be held accountable.
This is putting money first. This is putting profit first. And it's devastating.
A major construction project was taking place next to the building before the collapse,
and investigators are examining some of the debris left behind to help determine what caused it.
Doa Halit Saikavto, NPR News, in Brooklyn.
U.S. District Judge Anna Rises is temporarily blocking President Trump from closing a golf course along the Potomac River
that Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.
That means for now, the course remains open.
Under the plan, Trump had planned to close it tomorrow despite a legal challenge initiated against the project.
You're listening to NPR News.
A federal rule requiring stores that accept SNAP benefits to stock more fresh and perishable foods has been delayed
after going to effect earlier this month.
As Macy Byers reports, small grocers and convenience stores say it would be hard to comply with.
New York City Mayor Zoran Mamdani, in partnership with the National Association of Convenience Stores,
announced they had brokered a deal with President Trump for a 90-day delay.
Many small and rural grocery stores have opposed the new requirements, saying they may not have the resources to comply.
Carly Jonas with the Nebraska-based Center for Rural Affairs says that could lead stores to drop their SNAP retailer status.
They want to be able to have SNAP and people be able to access it because it does help support their business
and feed people in their community.
And it's just conflicting because they also are operating on such in-profit margins that they don't want to risk getting in trouble.
Supporters of the delay say it will give retailers more time to adjust.
For NPR News, I'm Macy Byers in Lincoln, Nebraska.
SpaceX made history today when it successfully caught a rocket after a 22-and-a-half-hour round trip ride to space.
The company's Starship spacecraft returned to its Texas launch pad in dramatic fashion
as the vehicle carefully lowered itself until two metal arms attached to the launch tower could grab it.
The maneuver is key to making the Starship quickly reusable, which is a critical part of SpaceX's future business plans.
Stocks getting ground this week with all three major indices rising more than 2 percent for the week.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Democrats gather in Denver for conference, with Pete Buttigieg urging a rapid-fire cost-of-living bill series
Over 10,000 flights delayed or canceled after a federal contractor's work may have caused a system reboot
Brooklyn building collapse kills at least eight; crews remove rubble and investigators examine debris
Judge Anna Rises temporarily blocks Trump from closing Potomac River golf course for redevelopment
Federal SNAP rule requiring fresh food stock is delayed 90 days after small grocers object
SpaceX catches its Starship rocket with launch tower arms after a 22.5-hour round trip to space
Stocks rise over 2 percent for the week as all three major indices gain
